sections.text: Ownership is how Rust manages memory without a garbage collector and without you freeing memory by hand. It rests on three rules.
1. Every value has an owner, usually a variable. 2. There is only one owner at a time. 3. When the owner goes out of scope, the value is dropped (its memory is freed).
A String stores its text on the heap. When you assign it to another variable, ownership moves. The old variable can't be used any more:
The heap is memory a program asks for while it runs, for data like text that can grow. That memory has to be given back when it's no longer needed, and ownership is how Rust decides when.

Passing a String to a function moves it too (the next lesson shows types that are copied instead). The parameter becomes the new owner, and the caller can't use the value any more. A function can hand ownership to its caller by returning a value. Here shout returns a brand-new String, and loud owns it:
What if you want to keep using a value after a function has used it? Instead of giving it away, you can lend it. That's called borrowing, and it's two lessons from now.
Think of it like handing someone a physical book. Once you've given it away, you don't have it any more. That's how Rust knows exactly when it's safe to free memory.

A move is a cheap shallow copy of the pointer, length and capacity; the heap data isn't copied. Because only one owner exists, there's no double free and no need for reference counting. C++ programmers: a Rust move is the default, the compiler forbids any later use of the old variable, and the old variable isn't dropped (only the new owner is). A moved-from C++ object stays alive and its destructor still runs later; standard-library types are left in a valid but unspecified state.

exercise.prompt:
The program uses name after it was moved into greet. Change greet so it doesn't need to own the String: make the parameter a reference (&String) and call it with &name. A reference lets greet borrow the String instead of owning it; you'll learn how references work in the Borrowing lesson of this unit. It should print: Hello, Ferris
Bye, Ferris

tests.label: greet prints Hello, Ferris
tests.code:
let name = String::from("Ferris");
check_eq!(output_of(|| greet(&name)), "Hello, Ferris\n");

tests.label: The String is still usable after greet
The program prints Hello, then Bye
a name a hard-coded Ferris would not match
tests.code:
let name = String::from("Ann");
check_eq!(output_of(|| greet(&name)), "Hello, Ann\n");

tests.label: spaces in the name
tests.code:
let name = String::from("Ferris the crab");
check_eq!(output_of(|| greet(&name)), "Hello, Ferris the crab\n");

tests.label: an empty name, still borrowed

hints: Passing name to greet moves it, so main can't use it afterwards. Let greet borrow it instead.
A reference lets a function borrow a value. In the parameter list, put & before the type. In the call, put & before the variable.
Change the parameter to name: &String. Then call greet(&name) in main. The tests call greet(&name) too, so the parameter has to take a reference; .clone() would not fit them.

quiz.question: How many owners can a value have at one time?
quiz.explanation: Every value has exactly one owner at a time. That rule is how Rust knows when to free the memory: when the single owner goes away, the value is dropped.

quiz.question: What happens to a value when its owner goes out of scope?
options: It's dropped and its memory freed
It stays until the program ends
quiz.explanation: When the owner goes out of scope, Rust drops the value and frees its memory right there, with no garbage collector. The value does not live on until the program ends, and it does not move to main.

quiz.question: After let b = a; where a is a String, can you still use a?
quiz.explanation: let b = a; moves the String from a to b. Now b is the owner, and using a fails to compile, even just to print it. Only integers and other Copy types stay usable after being assigned.
